newsitem.title: USA: Stocks battered by report, interest-rate worries.
newsitem.headline: Stocks battered by report, interest-rate worries.

text.p: Stocks started 1997 the way they ended 1996: falling on investor worries about higher interest rates.
Thursday's drop came after a report that showed robust manufacturing activity in December sparked a steep decline in the inflation-sensitive bond market, which in turn hurt stocks.

At 1 p.m., the Dow Jones industrial average was off 40.80 points at 6,407.47 after falling as much as 95 points earlier. In the broader market, declining issues outnumbered gainers by better than 3-1 on moderate New York Stock Exchange volume of about 266 million shares.
The drop came after the Dow fell 101 points on Tuesday.

Analysts said the declines might signal the start of a tough year for stocks. The market rose 26 percent in 1996 and 33.5 percent in 1995 as measured by the Dow, back-to-back gains seen only twice before in the market's history.
"We have to keep perspective. We've had a huge run-up, there was a record all-time high Monday," said Tom Carpenter, chief economist at ASB Capital Management, referring to the Dow.

The report that sparked the sell-off came from the National Association of Purchasing Management, which said its index of maufacturing activity rose to 54.0 in December, the highest in six months, from 52.7 in November. A reading above 50 points to growth in manufacturing, while one below that level indicates contraction.

The report, the first broad glimpse of the economy each month, signalled a pickup in economic growth that could lead to accelerating inflation and higher interest rates, traders and analysts said. The group's index stood at 54.3 in June.
It was the first major indicator of the new year and had been widely awaited in financial markets. Private economists had expected a reading of 51.5 for December.

The group also said its index of prices paid rose last month to its highest level in 17 months. So far, most price increases have been absorbed by manufacturers and retailers and have not been not passed on, helping keep consumer price inflation tame.
But bond investors, keenly sensitive to signs of inflation that could erode the returns on their long-term investments, sent prices tumbling after the report.
The 30-year Treasury fell 1-1/4 points, or $12.50 on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.74 percent from 6.64 percent on Tuesday. Bond prices and yields move in the opposite direction.
The steep drop in stock prices on Tuesday followed reports of a strong rise in consumer confidence in December and the fastest rise in new home sales in November in 3-1/2 years.
While Tuesday's drop was confined mostly to blue-chip issues, Thursday's decline moved beyond into the broader market.

The Nasdaq composite index and the Russell 2000 index of smaller stocks, both of which managed slight gains on Tuesday, fell more sharply than the 30-share Dow average, which was off about 0.6 percent.
The Russell 2000 index fell 4.35 to 358.26, losing 1.20 percent of its value. The Nasdaq composite, heavily weighted with technology stocks, fell 10.68 to 1,280.35, off about 0.83 percent.

The slide in stocks erased moderate opening gains. The major indexes had risen slightly at the opening after the Labour Department's report of a rise in jobless claims last week helped quell fears of too much economic strength that could fuel a pickup in interest rates.
The department said new unemployment claims rose to 366,000 last week compared to a revised 344,000 in the prior week. Estimates had been for claims of about 334,000.
Carpenter said the rise in jobless claims could work against the stock market since weakness in the labour market could reinforce worries about weaker corporate earnings.
The American Stock Exchange index fell 3.53 to 568.81.
Financial markets were closed on Wednesday for New Year's Day.
